# The Game That Could Redefine Its Category

# 1. Vision

This game is being created with one simple ambition: **to become the kind of experience that makes players rethink what a great game can be.**

Although its final genre and exact category are still being defined, that uncertainty is not a limitation. It is an opportunity. Instead of designing around a rigid formula, the game can take the strongest qualities from different kinds of interactive experiences and combine them into something that feels fresh, memorable, and unmistakably its own.

The goal is not simply to make a game that looks impressive. The goal is to create a game that players *feel*.

Every major element should contribute to that feeling: the world, gameplay, atmosphere, characters, sound, visuals, progression, surprises, and the sense that the player's actions genuinely matter. The experience should constantly encourage the player to think, explore, experiment, and continue playing because they genuinely want to know what happens next.

# 2. Designed to Stand Above the Competition

The ambition for this project is significantly higher than simply being "good for an indie game" or "good for its genre."

It should aim to compete with the expectations normally associated with major AAA releases.

That means pursuing exceptional quality across the entire experience rather than relying on one impressive feature. A beautiful game with weak gameplay is not enough. A technically advanced game without personality is not enough. A game with great mechanics but no emotional impact is not enough.

The objective is to bring these qualities together.

The game should feel polished from the moment players begin. Menus, controls, animation, environments, sound design, interactions, pacing, feedback, and progression should all communicate that considerable care has gone into the experience.

Most importantly, the game should develop its own identity.

Players should be able to experience it for a few minutes and eventually say, **"This feels like that game."**

# 3. A World Players Want to Enter

One of the game's greatest strengths should be its ability to create curiosity.

The player should constantly have reasons to look around the next corner, investigate something unusual, discover another location, experiment with a mechanic, or simply remain in the world because it is enjoyable to exist there.

Rather than overwhelming players with unnecessary content, the experience should focus on meaningful details.

Small discoveries can become memorable moments. Environmental details can tell stories without forcing exposition. Characters can feel like more than quest dispensers. Locations can have their own personality.

The world should feel designed rather than filled.

# 4. Gameplay That Feels Exceptional

Regardless of the final genre, the fundamental interaction needs to feel satisfying.

Controls should be responsive. Actions should have weight. Feedback should be clear. Success should feel earned, while failure should encourage another attempt rather than frustration.

The game should reward different kinds of players. Someone who enjoys mastery should find depth. Someone who enjoys exploration should find secrets. Someone who values story should discover meaningful moments. Someone who simply wants to have fun should be able to enjoy the experience without needing to understand every underlying system.

This flexibility can become one of the project's greatest advantages.

# 5. The AAA Comparison

The ultimate ambition is for players to experience the game and genuinely feel that it belongs in conversations with some of the biggest games ever produced.

This does **not** mean claiming that the game has objectively surpassed established AAA titles before release. Instead, the aspiration is that individual players may come away believing that it did.

A handful of passionate playtesters saying, *"I enjoyed this more than the latest AAA release I played,"* could be more meaningful than any marketing slogan.

The strongest possible reaction would be surprise.

Players might begin the experience expecting something interesting and finish it thinking they have discovered something extraordinary.

# 6. Test Player Perspective

One early test-player reaction could capture the emotional target of the project:

>

This kind of reaction represents the standard the project should strive toward.

The goal is not simply to make players acknowledge that the game is technically impressive. The goal is to make them **care about it**.

# 7. Building Something Memorable

Great games are remembered for more than graphics or review scores.

They are remembered because of moments.

A surprising discovery. An unforgettable character. A difficult decision. A breathtaking environment. A mechanic that nobody expected. A sequence that players talk about with friends years later.

This game should deliberately create opportunities for those moments.

Its strongest features should not exist only to impress during a trailer. They should remain memorable after the screen goes dark.

# 8. The Bigger Ambition

The most exciting aspect of the project is that its final identity does not need to be completely predetermined.

The genre can evolve.

The mechanics can evolve.

The presentation can evolve.

What should remain constant is the ambition: **make something players genuinely love.**

If the development process succeeds, the game will not need to repeatedly tell people that it is special. Players will do that themselves.

The ultimate measure of success would be seeing people recommend it enthusiastically, discuss its details, compare their experiences, create theories, replay it, and tell other people that they need to experience it.

# Conclusion

This project should aim to be more than another entry in a category.

It should aim to become a game that people remember.

A game that surprises players with its quality.

A game that can stand beside much larger productions and still feel confident in its identity.

A game that inspires some players to say that they enjoyed it more than games created with enormous AAA budgets.

And, most importantly, a game that earns those statements through the quality of the experience itself.

The genre may not have a name yet.

The category may not be completely defined.

But the ambition is clear:

**Create something so compelling, polished, imaginative, and enjoyable that players stop caring what category it belongs to — and simply call it one of the best games they've ever played.**

comments.author: chmillout
comments.body:
AI gamedev is under anti-ai crusade radar, this is the new witchhunt.

Therefore our duty in this sub is to make really good and polished games with AI, and not showing off how fast AI gamedev is. 

Your game looks cool but the philosophy should be: 

What awesome mechanics can you come up with AI? 

What solutions it provides that were not possible before? 

How much polish and cleanup is possible even though it is AI?

Yeah, main focus unfortunately is to actually cover the presence of AI so players won’t get the another slop impression. Once we learn how to pass this threshold - AI gamedev will become a completely normal way to make games and open doors to many awesome inspired projects.

So the main goal is to get the the player to think: 

1. “Hmmm I wonder if it is AI or not… can’t tell”  
2. “Woah If this game is made with AI tools then I am fine with it because the game is actually fun to play!”

Thats how we break the stigma.

And the worst thing AI devs can do is to spam 100s of poorly made games, and flood steam, itch.io and appstore because “hey we can stamp it so fast and make money on ads or kids because kids don’t care”

I think it depends on dev’s personal standards, like what your personal standards and goals are are, and what do you want to gift to the audience. So mindset is very important here.

Good luck and keep going! Just focus on polishing vs speed.
